new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19 pp., Chula Digital Collections scan, no text) and rendered PDF pages 2, 9 and 10 (printed pp. 126, 133, 134) to PNG and read them on the image, cross-checked against the held tesseract scanned. The passage is on p. 134 (PDF page 10), in the section headed THE VOWEL SYSTEM (which begins p. 133), as the entry for the sixth monophthong, exactly as quoted: "ə : represents a vowel that is lowered from Cardinal Vowel 19. It is a variant of [a] and it occurs only in an unstressed syllable." followed by the example line "tə⁵ wan¹ or ta⁵ wan¹ 'the sun'". Verbatim match (the only differences are scanned artefacts in the., not in the page scan). I read the whole article via scanned: consona…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated. The source describes Chiang Mai Tai Yuan as a six-tone language and mentions stress only in passing: the reduced vowel [ə] is confined to unstressed syllables, and the sole example is the minor first syllable of the disyllable tə⁵wan¹ 'sun' (a Standard-Thai-type sesquisyllable). This implies that in such words the first (minor) syllable is unstressed and the final full syllable carries the stress, as in Standard Thai, but the author does not say so explicitly and gives no statement for other polysyllables.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the alternation tə⁵wan¹ ~ ta⁵wan¹ shows the unstressed vowel may or may not reduce.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical disyllable in citation form); nothing on phrase-level stress or intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Woranoot 1976) describes the Chiang Mai variety of Kam Mueang (the author's own speech), i.e. the central sub-dialect of nort2740. Other opened sources cover Phrae, Lamphun, Chiang Rai, Nan, Chiang Saen (Jones 1965; Katsura 1969) and the Mae Sot/Tak sub-dialect (Sarawit 1979); all are silent on stress. No separate glottocode applies.

new_statements.quote: The phonological word in Nan dialect may have from one to four syllables. It has only one strongly stressed syllable which always occupies the last position, and may optionally have one to three preceding unstressed or weakly stressed syllables. [p. 33] ... There is only one strong stress in each word, that is the stress which occurs on the peak of monosyllabic word and on the last syllable of a polysyllabic word. Moreover, the weak stress and the unstress will occur only in other positions of these polysyllabic words. [p. 40] ... Since stress is predictable, stress markers will be left out in phonemic writing. [p. 43]

Moreover, the weak stress and the unstress will occur…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for nort2740 has an empty rule and the only existing statement (Woranoot 1976, Chiang Mai speech) says just that [ə] 'occurs only in an unstressed syllable' (tə⁵ wan¹ 'sun'). Chotecheun is compatible with that (her disyllabic type A, presyllable + major syllable, is stressed U.S, e.g. [pa 33. 'la:t 31] 'slippery', p. 41) and adds what the catalog lacks: the placement (always the last syllable of the phonological word), three degrees of stress, the presyllable/minor-syllable distinction, predictability and non-phonemic status, and the word domain (1-4 syllables). It describes the Nan (Pua district) variety, not Chiang Mai.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Nan (Pua) variety of Northern Thai the phonological word has one to four syllables and exactly one strong stress, always on its last syllable (the only syllable of a monosyllable). Every preceding syllable is either an unstressed presyllable ([Ca], reduced from /Ca:T/, p. 40 footnote) or a weakly stressed 'minor' syllable of full shape. Stress is 'predictable from the position of stress in a word and from the syllable structure' (p. 40), so it is non-contrastive and omitted from phonemic transcription. The dialect is tonal with six contrastive tones (p. 115), so this is a tone language with predictable word-final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A three-degree system: strong stress (marked '), weak stress (marked ˘) and unstress (unmarked), pp. 33, 40. Weak stress falls on non-final full syllables; attested patterns are S, U.S, W.S, U.W.S, W.U.S, U.W.U.S, U.W.W.S and W.W.W.S (pp. 40-43). p. 41: a weakly stressed syllable 'has the same structure as the strongly stressed syllable' and 'may be dropped in the utterances'; p. 43: 'In actual speed atterances, the weakly stressed may be dropped, leaving only one strongly stressed syllable.'
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions to final strong stress are stated; p. 43 concedes that weak stress or unstress may occur more than once in a polysyllable but 'words in Nan dialect bear only one strongly stress'. Phrase level: pp. 27-28 exclude the intonation group as non-phonemic, noting it 'depends on the tone of the final word of the stress group'. The Nan-Phrae comparison (Ch. 5) covers consonants, vowels and tones only; nothing on stress in Phrae.
new_statements.identity_note: Chotecheun 1986 describes the Nan dialect spoken at Ban Rong, Tambon Pua, Amphoe Pua, Nan Province (Abstract; p. 21), which she classifies as 'one of the Northern Thai (or Lanna) dialects' within Southwestern Tai (pp. 20-26) = nort2740. The Phrae comparison uses data from Phitsri Chaengphrai's 1977 Chulalongkorn MA thesis and covers consonants, vowels and tones only. The existing catalog statement (Woranoot 1976) is Chiang Mai speech.

tone_statements.translation: Northern Thai and Tai Lue have the same number of tonemes, namely 6 ... boxes A1 and A2, i.e. Tone 1: Northern Thai has a mid falling-rising tone (324) ... A3 and A4, i.e. Tone 2: Northern Thai has a mid level tone (333) ... B1, B2, B3, i.e. Tone 3: Northern Thai has a mid falling tone (322) ... B4, i.e. Tone 4: Northern Thai has a high falling tone (421) ... C1, C2, C3, i.e. Tone 5: Northern Thai has a high-mid falling tone (431) ... C4, i.e. Tone 6: Northern Thai has a mid rising tone (344).

tone_statements.citation: Intajamornrak, Chommanad. 2009. The Fundamental Frequencies of Tai Yuan Tones Spoken by Lua' (Mal) Speakers in Nan Province, Thailand. MANUSYA: Journal of Humanities 12(3): 20-33. Bangkok: Chulalongkorn University / Brill. DOI 10.1163/26659077-01203002 (open:https://brill.com/view/journals/mnya/12/3/article-p20_2.xml)
tone_statements.quote: Tai Yuan has six tones, while Ta Luang Mal has only two pitches. ... Figure 1 clearly reveals the six tones of Tai Yuan: 1) low-rising, 2) mid-rising, 3) mid-level, 4) mid-falling, 5) high-level and 6) high-falling. There are four contour tones: low-rising (T1), mid-rising (T2), mid-falling (T4), and high-falling (T6). ... For the level tones, the mid-level (T3) begins at mid pitch and then falls slightly over the first 75% of the duration. The high-level (T5) has a contour similar to the mid-level (T3), but it starts at a higher pitch and falls slightly at the end.
tone_statements.summary: Six tones (2 level, 4 contour) from F0 of 3 female Pua speakers; Table 5 p.30 gives 24 35 33 31 44 452; only T2-T5 occur in checked syllables. Nothing on stress; L2 Mal speakers merge T3/T4.

Bangkok: Chulalongkorn University / Brill. DOI 10.1163/26659077-01203002 (open:https://brill.com/view/journals/mnya/12/3/article-p20_2.xml)
sources.quote: Tai Yuan has six tones, while Ta Luang Mal has only two pitches. ... Figure 1 clearly reveals the six tones of Tai Yuan: 1) low-rising, 2) mid-rising, 3) mid-level, 4) mid-falling, 5) high-level and 6) high-falling. There are four contour tones: low-rising (T1), mid-rising (T2), mid-falling (T4), and high-falling (T6). ... For the level tones, the mid-level (T3) begins at mid pitch and then falls slightly over the first 75% of the duration. The high-level (T5) has a contour similar to the mid-level (T3), but it starts at a higher pitch and falls slightly at the end.
sources.note: Six tones (2 level, 4 contour) from F0 of 3 female Pua speakers; Table 5 p.30 gives 24 35 33 31 44 452; only T2-T5 occur in checked syllables. Nothing on stress; L2 Mal speakers merge T3/T4.

sources.quote: Data from the two Lampang speakers and the two Chiang Rai speakers were compared with the MacCECIL program, revealing that both dialects divide the Gedney chart (recall Figure 3) into ten sections, as shown in Figure 5, below: ... Chiang Mai Kammuang divides up in the same configuration as Chiang Rai and Lampang, grouping A1 and A2, whereas Bangkok Thai (see Figure 4) “clumps” A2, A3 and A4 together--strong indication, by Gedney’s criteria, that a linguistic boundary has been crossed. ... The A1 tone shapes of all four speakers are essentially the same: a basic rising tone
sources.note: Instrumental (MacCECIL) Gedney-box study: Lampang = Chiang Rai; chart splits into ten boxes, A1/A2 grouped as one rising tone. No tone count in words on readable pages; pp.10-18 (B, C, D) unread.

sources.quote: Mid rising, as in Chiengrai (KAM MUANG) na: ... 334 ... Figure 4 shows representative tone systems of the Lān Nā type. ... All these Lān Nā type tone systems (other than Lao Ngaeo, Tāk Bai, and Nam Bac) share the following characteristics: 1. A-*ph is rising and starts lower than A-*b. ... 2. A-*b varies in contour but always starts higher than A-*ph ... 3. B-*ph is level or falling. ... 4. B-*b is falling. ... 5. At least one of the two C-tones is usually falling. 6. Usually, but not always, the C-tones are glottalized. ... Chiang Rāi (KAM MŲANG) (Brown) ... Chiang Mai (KAM MŲANG) (Brown)
